title: Trump: Israel murders Iranian scientist, protests call for Iran to attack the U.S.
description_short: Trump: Israel murders Iranian scientist, protests call for Iran to attack the U.S.
description_medium: On November 27, 2020, Iran’s top nuclear scientist, Mohsen Fakhrizadeh, was killed in a targeted attack attributed to Israel by multiple foreign intelligence agencies. Iranian protesters called for retaliation against the United States, which some Iranians believed was involved. The account says the attack used a remotely operated weapon and notes that former CIA director John Brennan urged Iran to wait for the next administration before responding.
description_long: Mohsen Fakhrizadeh, Iran’s top nuclear scientist, was killed in a targeted attack on November 27, 2020. The Trump File account says multiple foreign intelligence agencies attributed the operation to Israel, while some Iranians believed the United States was involved. It describes Iranian protesters demanding retaliation against the U.S. and says former CIA director John Brennan urged Iran to wait until the next administration before deciding how to respond. Later reporting cited by the page described a satellite-operated, remotely controlled weapon, but the precise operational details were not part of the immediate public account. The killing heightened tensions around Iran’s nuclear program during the final weeks of Donald Trump’s presidency. The entry also notes reporting that Israel had targeted Fakhrizadeh for years and that Israel and the United States were coordinating pressure on Iran. Those details provide context, but they do not establish U.S. participation in the killing. The incident illustrates how a targeted assassination can raise retaliation risks and complicate diplomatic choices during a presidential transition; the supplied record does not document a direct Iranian military response to this specific attack.

title: Iran's Fordow Nuclear Facility Struck — Deepest Bunker Buster Deployed
description_short: Iran's Fordow Nuclear Facility Struck — Deepest Bunker Buster Deployed
description_medium: During the June 2025 U.S.-Israeli strikes on Iran’s nuclear infrastructure, the Fordow enrichment facility was targeted with the U.S. GBU-57 Massive Ordnance Penetrator, according to the supplied account. The weapon is described as a 30,000-pound bunker buster designed for deeply buried facilities. Damage assessments suggested substantial harm but left open whether the site was destroyed.
description_long: The supplied account says the Fordow uranium-enrichment facility, located beneath a mountain near Qom, was targeted during the June 2025 U.S.-Israeli strikes on Iran. It describes use of the U.S. GBU-57 Massive Ordnance Penetrator, a 30,000-pound weapon designed to penetrate hardened underground facilities, and calls this its first operational combat use. The record says employment of the weapon required direct presidential authorization under strict protocols. Satellite imagery and intelligence assessments reportedly indicated significant damage, while leaving uncertain whether the facility had been completely destroyed. That uncertainty matters because the strikes were presented as an effort to damage Iran’s nuclear infrastructure, yet the available account does not establish that the site was eliminated or that the broader objective was achieved. The entry is dated June 13, the start of the wider conflict described in its source material, but the supplied synopsis does not give a separate date for the Fordow strike itself. The description therefore treats the targeting as part of the June campaign and preserves the unresolved damage assessment. It records the use of a powerful conventional weapon against a deeply protected nuclear site without asserting an outcome that the cited material does not confirm.

title: Donald Trump taps Matt Gaetz & Tulsi Gabbard for DOJ and National Intelligence
description_short: Donald Trump taps Matt Gaetz & Tulsi Gabbard for DOJ and National Intelligence
description_medium: On November 13, 2024, President-elect Donald Trump announced Matt Gaetz as his choice for attorney general and Tulsi Gabbard as his choice for director of national intelligence. The announcements were part of a series of selections for the incoming administration. Trump described Gaetz as a reformer at the Justice Department and praised Gabbard’s military service and intelligence role.
description_long: On November 13, 2024, Donald Trump announced Matt Gaetz as his selection for attorney general and Tulsi Gabbard as his selection for director of national intelligence. The announcements came amid a broader round of choices for the administration he was preparing to form, including the previously announced government-efficiency initiative led by Elon Musk and Vivek Ramaswamy. Trump’s statement praised Gaetz and said he would bring honesty, integrity, and transparency to the Justice Department. He described Gabbard as a former congresswoman and Army lieutenant colonel and said she would lead the intelligence community. These were consequential personnel choices: the attorney general leads the Justice Department, while the director of national intelligence coordinates the U.S. intelligence community. The selection of political allies for those posts drew attention because each role carries substantial responsibility for law enforcement or national security. This entry records the announcements and Trump’s public rationale, not the eventual confirmation or service of either candidate. It does not supply enough detail to evaluate the full record of objections to the nominees, so no additional claims about those controversies are included here.

title: Donald Trump: Be nice to my murderous, armed supporters as they storm your offices
description_short: Donald Trump: Be nice to my murderous, armed supporters as they storm your offices
description_medium: On May 1, 2020, after armed demonstrators entered Michigan’s Capitol and threatened police and Governor Gretchen Whitmer, President Trump praised them as “very good people.” He urged Whitmer to negotiate and “put out the fire,” while saying the protesters wanted their lives back safely. The post followed weeks of Trump and allies criticizing Michigan’s COVID-19 restrictions.
description_long: On May 1, 2020, President Donald Trump tweeted in support of armed demonstrators who had entered the Michigan State Capitol and threatened police officers and Governor Gretchen Whitmer. He called them “very good people,” said they were angry and wanted their lives back safely, and urged Whitmer to “give a little” and make a deal. The post followed weeks of criticism from Trump and his allies of Michigan’s COVID-19 precautions. The timeline says some people around Trump had helped organize armed protests in multiple states, but this entry focuses on his public response after the Michigan protest. Praising the demonstrators while asking the governor to negotiate gave political validation to an armed confrontation over public-health rules. The statement came as state officials were enforcing restrictions during the pandemic and facing pressure to reopen. This account records Trump’s words and the circumstances described by the source; it does not claim that the tweet alone caused the protest or establish the intent of every person who entered the Capitol. The episode remains notable for the president’s response to threats directed at elected officials and law enforcement.

title: Trump: Channel 4: Trump campaign had data on 200 million voters, targeted Black voters in 2016
description_short: Trump: Channel 4: Trump campaign had data on 200 million voters, targeted Black voters in 2016
description_medium: A Channel 4 News investigation published on September 28, 2020 reported that the 2016 Trump campaign used data on nearly 200 million Americans to target voters online. It found that about 3.5 million Black voters were labeled “Deterrence,” a category associated with people the campaign hoped would not vote. The campaign denied targeting Black voters, and the available ad record was incomplete.
description_long: A Channel 4 News investigation published on September 28, 2020 reported that the 2016 Trump campaign, working with the Republican National Committee and Cambridge Analytica, used data on nearly 200 million Americans for targeted digital advertising. The investigation said about 3.5 million Black Americans were placed in a “Deterrence” category and described campaign material aimed at discouraging support for Hillary Clinton. Channel 4 reported that the category included disproportionate numbers of Black voters in several battleground states and cited a campaign data scientist’s description of the audience as people the campaign hoped would not turn out. The campaign denied specifically targeting Black voters. The source also cautioned that many Facebook ads were temporary “dark posts,” and no complete public archive existed to show exactly which voters received which messages. The episode raised concerns about using voter data and targeted advertising to suppress participation, particularly among Black Americans. The reporting presents evidence of a strategy and campaign audience categories, but the missing ad archive limits a complete account of delivery to individual voters. This description attributes the findings and the campaign’s denial to the reporting rather than treating every intended or actual effect as independently established.

title: Trump Withdraws from Paris Agreement and Pauses WTO Contributions
description_short: Trump Withdraws from Paris Agreement and Pauses WTO Contributions
description_medium: On January 20, 2025, Donald Trump ordered the United States to withdraw again from the Paris climate agreement and revoked the U.S. International Climate Finance Plan. A UN notice followed on January 27. By March, Reuters reported that the administration had paused U.S. contributions to the World Trade Organization for 2024 and 2025; the account also says it halted WHO pandemic-agreement negotiations.
description_long: On January 20, 2025, Donald Trump signed Executive Order 14162 directing the United States to withdraw from the Paris Agreement, beginning a second withdrawal process. The United Nations issued a depositary notification on January 27. The same account says Trump revoked the U.S. International Climate Finance Plan, ending funding commitments intended to support developing nations. It also reports that by March 28 the administration had paused U.S. contributions to the World Trade Organization for 2024 and 2025, despite the United States being the organization’s largest contributor, and halted negotiations on the World Health Organization’s Pandemic Agreement. These actions affected several forms of multilateral cooperation: climate commitments, trade institution funding, and pandemic planning. The reported WTO pause raised concerns about the organization’s operations, while the climate withdrawal reduced U.S. participation in a global framework. The synopsis attributes these steps to the administration but does not detail the legal timetable for each withdrawal or the full operational effects of the funding pause. The entry describes a broader retreat from international agreements and institutions rather than one isolated policy change, while retaining the dates and limits stated in the supplied reporting.

title: Trump's Doha Agreement Sets Stage for Taliban Takeover of Afghanistan
description_short: Trump's Doha Agreement Sets Stage for Taliban Takeover of Afghanistan
description_medium: The February 2020 Doha Agreement committed the United States to withdraw all troops from Afghanistan by May 2021 in exchange for Taliban counterterrorism assurances. The Trump administration negotiated directly with the Taliban without including Afghanistan’s elected government and agreed to release 5,000 Taliban prisoners. After President Biden carried out the withdrawal in August 2021, the Afghan government collapsed rapidly.
description_long: The Doha Agreement, signed in February 2020 by the Trump administration and the Taliban, set a timetable for withdrawing U.S. forces from Afghanistan by May 2021 in return for Taliban promises not to harbor terrorists. The agreement was negotiated without Afghanistan’s elected government as a party, a choice the supplied account says weakened Kabul’s legitimacy. It also provided for the release of 5,000 Taliban prisoners, including commanders who later participated in the Taliban’s military campaign. President Biden carried out the final U.S. withdrawal in August 2021, after which the Afghan government collapsed within days and the Taliban took control. This sequence distinguishes the agreement Trump negotiated from the withdrawal Biden executed. The source argues that excluding Kabul and releasing prisoners created conditions that made the later collapse more likely; that is a causal interpretation of the agreement’s effects, not proof that the February deal alone determined what happened in 2021. The agreement nevertheless shaped the commitments and political conditions inherited by the next administration. The entry focuses on those provisions and their consequences for the Afghan government’s position during the transition and withdrawal.

title: Trump Pardons All Jan 6 Defendants Including Seditious Conspiracy Convicts
description_short: Trump Pardons All Jan 6 Defendants Including Seditious Conspiracy Convicts
description_medium: On January 20, 2025, his first day back in office, President Trump issued pardons or commutations for virtually all defendants charged in connection with the January 6 Capitol attack. The action included people convicted of seditious conspiracy, including leaders of the Proud Boys and Oath Keepers. Families of injured officers expressed outrage, while critics said the clemency rewarded political violence.
description_long: On January 20, 2025, the first day of his second term, President Donald Trump issued pardons and commutations covering virtually all defendants charged or convicted in connection with the January 6, 2021 attack on the U.S. Capitol. The clemency reached more than 1,500 people, including members and leaders of the Proud Boys and Oath Keepers who had been convicted of serious offenses, including seditious conspiracy. Families of police officers injured during the attack expressed outrage. Critics argued that granting broad clemency signaled that political violence carried out in Trump’s name would be rewarded or protected. The action removed or reduced criminal penalties for people whose cases arose from an effort to disrupt Congress’s certification of the 2020 election. Its consequences therefore extended beyond individual sentences to questions of accountability for violence against elected representatives and law enforcement. The entry describes the scope and timing of Trump’s clemency and attributes the interpretation of its political message to critics. It does not suggest that every person covered had the same conduct or conviction; the source itself notes a wide group of defendants and distinguishes pardons from commutations.

title: Trump Attacks General Milley, Suggests He Could Be Executed for Treason
description_short: Trump Attacks General Milley, Suggests He Could Be Executed for Treason
description_medium: In a September 2022 Truth Social post, former President Trump called General Mark Milley’s calls to his Chinese counterpart after January 6 a “treasonous act” and said the offense “used to be” punishable by death. Milley was then chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff. Defense officials and legal experts criticized the rhetoric as dangerous to civil-military relations.
description_long: In September 2022, former President Donald Trump escalated his public criticism of General Mark Milley by writing on Truth Social that Milley’s calls to his Chinese counterpart after January 6 were a “treasonous act” that “used to be” punishable by death. Milley was serving as chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff at the time. The calls had been made during the crisis surrounding the January 6 attack; the supplied account characterizes them as lawful communication intended to maintain stability. Defense officials and legal experts condemned Trump’s language as dangerous to civil-military relations. The post did not constitute a government order or legal proceeding, but its execution-related rhetoric directed hostility at a senior military officer for conduct undertaken in an official capacity. The incident raised concerns about political leaders using accusations of treason and references to death against public servants who disagreed with them. The source says the episode was later cited in Justice Department filings as part of a broader pattern of hostility toward officials who crossed Trump. This entry documents the public statement and the criticism it drew without implying that Milley was charged with treason or that any execution was contemplated by the government.

title: Trump Pressures VP Pence to Reject Electoral Votes on January 6
description_short: Trump Pressures VP Pence to Reject Electoral Votes on January 6
description_medium: In the weeks before January 6, 2021, President Trump pressured Vice President Mike Pence to reject or delay certification of electoral votes for Joe Biden. Trump claimed Pence could send contested votes back to states, although the supplied account says that authority had no basis in law. Pence refused and stated that the Constitution did not give him that power.
description_long: In the weeks leading up to January 6, 2021, President Donald Trump and his allies pressured Vice President Mike Pence to reject or delay the counting of electoral votes that confirmed Joe Biden’s victory. Trump argued that Pence could return votes from contested states, even though the supplied account says the Constitution and law gave the vice president no such authority. On the morning of January 6, Trump publicly criticized Pence for not taking the action he demanded and repeated the claim at the Stop the Steal rally shortly before the attack on the Capitol. Pence refused and released a letter explaining that his role did not include unilateral power to reject electoral votes. The pressure campaign targeted the formal congressional process for transferring presidential power. Its timing and repeated claims increased pressure on Pence and heightened the danger surrounding the certification session. The entry records the demand, Pence’s refusal, and the immediate institutional context; it does not treat the vice president’s role as discretionary or the election claims as valid. The episode is a central example of efforts to interfere with certification of the 2020 election result.
